shortExplanation: The boat must devote 4 m/s of its water-relative velocity to canceling the current. Its remaining eastward component is 3 m/s, giving a 200-second crossing.
detailedSteps: Choose east and north as positive. The water velocity is $(0,-4)$ m/s, so the boat needs a northward component of $4$ m/s through the water.
Its fixed speed gives $u_x^2+4^2=5^2$. The eastward component is $u_x=3\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
The ground velocity is consequently $(3,0)$ m/s. Crossing the $600$-meter width takes $t=600/3=200\,\mathrm{s}$.
keyIdeas: Add velocities as vectors.
commonMistakes: Do not divide the width by the boat speed relative to the water; that speed is directed partly upstream.
difficultyNotes: The required ground direction determines the heading before the crossing time.

shortExplanation: Add the two travel times and divide the total 100-kilometer distance by that sum. The result is about 55.17 km/h.
detailedSteps: The elapsed time is $T=25/80+75/50=29/16\,\mathrm{h}$.
Therefore $\bar s=100/(29/16)=1600/29=55.1724\ldots\,\mathrm{km/h}$, closest to $55.2$.
keyIdeas: Average speed uses total distance and total elapsed time.
commonMistakes: An arithmetic mean gives equal weight to the two speeds even though their travel times differ.
difficultyNotes: All motion has the same direction, so no displacement cancellation is involved.

shortExplanation: At a steady speed, the engine supplies the drag force times speed. Quadratic drag therefore makes required power proportional to the cube of speed.
detailedSteps: Force balance gives thrust $F=kv^2$. Its power is $P=Fv=kv^3$.
With the same drag constant, $2P_0/P_0=(v/v_0)^3$. Hence $v=2^{1/3}v_0=1.2599\ldots v_0$.
keyIdeas: Power is force times speed.
commonMistakes: The extra factor of speed in the power relation makes the cube root necessary.
difficultyNotes: This compares the steady operating speeds, rather than the transient acceleration after the power change.

shortExplanation: The initially stationary box stays at rest until static friction is exceeded. Kinetic friction is smaller, so acceleration begins with a positive jump and then grows linearly.
detailedSteps: For a nonzero static coefficient, the starting threshold is $P_s=\mu_s mg$. For independently applied forces $P\leq P_s$, static friction balances the force and $a=0$.
Once sliding starts, the opposing force is $P_k=\mu_kmg=0.90P_s$, so $a=(P-P_k)/m$.
Just above $P_s$, the acceleration tends to $(P_s-P_k)/m=0.10\mu_s g$. After that its slope with respect to $P$ is $1/m$.

Graph A has the stationary plateau, a modest positive jump, and a line whose extrapolated zero is below the static threshold. The drawings are schematic; their pixel scales are not numerical measurements.
keyIdeas: Static friction adjusts below its limit; kinetic friction has the smaller fixed magnitude.
commonMistakes: A continuous transition would correspond to equal static and kinetic coefficients. A positive acceleration at zero applied force contradicts an initially resting box.
difficultyNotes: The graph describes trials starting from rest. In the degenerate frictionless limit, the plateau and jump collapse to the line $a=P/m$.

shortExplanation: The figure marks 150 meters along the initial line of aim. The ball reaches the wall in 1.5 seconds and falls 11.25 meters below the target.
detailedSteps: The dotted target distance has horizontal projection $x=150\cos60^\circ=75\,\mathrm{m}$. It is not a $150$-meter horizontal distance.
The horizontal speed is $100\cos60^\circ=50\,\mathrm{m/s}$, so the wall is reached after $t=75/50=1.5\,\mathrm{s}$.
Without gravity the ball would follow the line of aim to the target. Gravity lowers its height by $gt^2/2=10(1.5)^2/2=11.25\,\mathrm{m}$, nearest the listed $11$ meters.
keyIdeas: Read the orientation of a dimension line before resolving the trajectory.
commonMistakes: Using 150 meters as the horizontal distance ignores the explicit dotted dimension in the original figure.
difficultyNotes: Mass does not enter ideal projectile motion; the supplied diagram determines the flight time.

shortExplanation: All collisions are internal to the three-cart system. Its total horizontal momentum and mass determine the same center-of-mass velocity before and after them.
detailedSteps: Taking right as positive, $p=1.9(1.7)+1.1(-2.5)+1.3(0)=0.48\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.
The mass is $1.9+1.1+1.3=4.3\,\mathrm{kg}$. Thus $V_{\rm CM}=0.48/4.3=0.1116\ldots\,\mathrm{m/s}$ to the right.
The frictionless track supplies no external horizontal impulse. Inelastic collisions may reduce kinetic energy, but they do not alter this center-of-mass result.
keyIdeas: Use a conserved whole-system quantity instead of following every collision.
commonMistakes: The two initially moving carts have opposite signed momenta.
difficultyNotes: Neither the number nor the ordering of later collisions is needed.

shortExplanation: The first two carts stick and continue rightward, then catch the third. All three eventually share the original momentum over a total mass of 13m.
detailedSteps: After the first capture, the combined $4m$ mass moves at $mv_0/(4m)=v_0/4>0$. It therefore catches stationary cart C.
The final mass is $(1+3+9)m=13m$. Momentum conservation gives $13mV=mv_0$, so $V=v_0/13$.
keyIdeas: Confirm that the intermediate object can reach the next cart.
commonMistakes: Cart C does not receive all the original momentum as an isolated 9m body; the other carts remain attached.
difficultyNotes: The positive intermediate velocity makes the stated final capture physically attainable.

shortExplanation: The first elastic collision gives cart B half the original speed. Its collision with the nine-times-heavier cart gives C one quarter of the original speed, and no further collision occurs.
detailedSteps: For an elastic collision with a stationary target, the incoming body has final velocity $u_1=(m_1-m_2)u/(m_1+m_2)$ and the target has final velocity $u_2=2m_1u/(m_1+m_2)$.
Apply this to masses $m,3m$: $u_A=-v_0/2$ and $u_B=v_0/2$.
Apply it next to masses $3m,9m$ with incoming speed $v_0/2$: $u_B=-v_0/4$ and $u_C=v_0/4$.
At that point A is left of B and has the more negative velocity. Their separation increases; B and C also separate. The ordered velocities $-v_0/2<-v_0/4<v_0/4$ exclude later collisions.
keyIdeas: An answer after one impact is final only when subsequent collision possibilities are checked.
commonMistakes: Do not combine all three masses into one object for an elastic sequence.
difficultyNotes: Checking the final ordering supplies the missing last-collision justification.

shortExplanation: The two final momentum vectors are perpendicular, so their squared magnitudes add to the square of the initial momentum.
detailedSteps: The initial momentum magnitude is $0.650(5.00)=3.25\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$; the second ball ends with magnitude $0.750(4.00)=3.00\,\mathrm{kg\,m/s}$.
The right-angle condition gives $(0.650u)^2+3.00^2=3.25^2$. Hence $0.650u=1.25$ and $u=25/13=1.9231\ldots\,\mathrm{m/s}$.
keyIdeas: Apply the right-angle condition to momentum vectors.
commonMistakes: Adding their magnitudes linearly would require collinear final directions.
difficultyNotes: The supplied final directions fix the speed without an elastic-collision assumption.

shortExplanation: The actual final speeds give less kinetic energy than initially, while the final energy remains positive. That places the change strictly between minus the initial energy and zero.
detailedSteps: Using the preceding result $u=25/13\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $K_i=\tfrac12(0.650)(5.00)^2=65/8\,\mathrm{J}$.
Therefore $\Delta K=K_f-K_i=-12/13\,\mathrm{J}<0$. Since $K_f>0$, we also have $\Delta K>-K_i$.
keyIdeas: Calculate energy from the stated velocities; momentum conservation alone does not conserve energy.
commonMistakes: Perpendicular outgoing directions do not by themselves establish a perfectly elastic collision for unequal masses.
difficultyNotes: The strict inequalities follow from the positive final energy and its computed loss.

shortExplanation: Floating in water determines the sphere density. Dividing that density by the lower oil density gives a submerged fraction of 8/9.
detailedSteps: Buoyant equilibrium in water gives $\rho_s=(2/3)\rho_w$.
For oil density $\rho_o=(3/4)\rho_w$, equilibrium requires submerged fraction $\rho_s/\rho_o=(2/3)/(3/4)=8/9$.
This is less than one, so the sphere can indeed float in the oil.
keyIdeas: The submerged volume fraction equals the object-to-fluid density ratio.
commonMistakes: A lower-density fluid requires more submerged volume, not less.
difficultyNotes: The resulting fraction also checks the proposed floating state.

finalAnswer: $\boxed{\text{vertically upward acceleration at the bottom}}$ (choice E)
shortExplanation: At the bottom, the tangential component vanishes while the moving bob has inward centripetal acceleration. The inward direction there is vertically upward.
detailedSteps: For a genuine swing with $0<\theta_{\max}<90^\circ$, energy conservation gives $v^2/L=2g(\cos\theta-\cos\theta_{\max})$.
The acceleration has inward component $v^2/L$ and downhill tangential component $g\sin\theta$. At the bottom, $\theta=0$ and $v^2/L=2g(1-\cos\theta_{\max})>0$.
The resulting acceleration points upward. It equals $g$ only for the special amplitude $60^\circ$, so that magnitude is not a general conclusion.
No point of a nonzero swing has zero total acceleration: the interior has a positive radial component, and a turning point has a nonzero tangential component.
keyIdeas: Zero tangential acceleration does not mean zero total acceleration.
commonMistakes: The force of gravity alone is not the acceleration of a constrained pendulum.
difficultyNotes: The statement concerns direction; the bottom acceleration magnitude depends on the release angle.

shortExplanation: Combine inward acceleration with the downhill tangential component. Throughout the allowed release-angle range, the half-amplitude vector points left and up, tilted away from the purely radial direction.
detailedSteps: Write $\theta=\theta_{\max}/2$, so $0<\theta<45^\circ$. On the right side, inward direction is $(-\sin\theta,\cos\theta)$ and downhill tangential direction is $(-\cos\theta,-\sin\theta)$.
Energy gives $a_r=2g(\cos\theta-\cos2\theta)$, while $a_t=g\sin\theta$. Both components are nonzero.
The horizontal component is $a_x=-a_r\sin\theta-g\sin\theta\cos\theta<0$.
Put $c=\cos\theta>1/\sqrt2$. The vertical component factors as $$\frac{a_y}{g}=2c(c-\cos2\theta)-\sin^2\theta=(1-c)(4c^2+c-1)>0.$$ The last quadratic is positive over this entire range.
The vector thus points up and left, with a downhill-tangent contribution that rules out the purely inward arrow A. The corresponding actual option is D.
keyIdeas: Resolve a curved-motion acceleration into radial and tangential parts.
Prove the vertical sign over the full allowed angle interval.
commonMistakes: The bob is moving uphill, but its tangential acceleration is downhill. Its velocity arrow is therefore not its acceleration arrow.
difficultyNotes: A numerical example alone would not establish the direction for every permitted amplitude.

shortExplanation: Each mass is 1.5 meters from the rotation center and feels one rope tension as its centripetal force.
detailedSteps: For either $5.0$-kg object, $T=m\omega^2r=5.0(4.0)^2(1.5)=120\,\mathrm{N}$.
The tension is the same along the massless rope. The equal forces acting on the two objects are not added to define a doubled rope tension.
keyIdeas: Apply the radial force equation to one object.
commonMistakes: The rod length is 3.0 meters, but each object has radius 1.5 meters.
difficultyNotes: The frictionless rod allows radial sliding; the original rope maintains the two stated radii.

shortExplanation: Angular momentum stays constant as the masses move inward. The motor supplies the increase in rotational kinetic energy, not the whole final energy.
detailedSteps: Initially $I_i=2(5)(1.5)^2=22.5\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$ and angular momentum is $H=I_i\omega_i=90\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2/s}$.
At the final radius, $I_f=2(5)(0.5)^2=2.5\,\mathrm{kg\,m^2}$, so $\omega_f=H/I_f=36\,\mathrm{rad/s}$.
The initial and final rotational energies are $K_i=I_i(4)^2/2=180\,\mathrm{J}$ and $K_f=I_f(36)^2/2=1620\,\mathrm{J}$.
Slow contraction makes radial endpoint kinetic energy negligible. With no dissipation or external work about the center, the motor work is $K_f-K_i=1440\,\mathrm{J}$.
keyIdeas: Conserve angular momentum, then compare energies.
commonMistakes: Holding angular speed fixed would introduce an external torque absent from the setup.
alternativeMethods: Equivalently, $K=H^2/(2I)$ with the same conserved $H$ at both radii.
difficultyNotes: The stated slow tightening separates the final rotational energy from transient radial motion.

shortExplanation: Force is minus the potential slope, with the horizontal centimeter scale converted to meters. The acceleration near 2 cm is thousands of m/s², not 4 cm/s².
detailedSteps: The source graph has stationary points near $x=1$ cm and $x=3$ cm. Each can be an equilibrium position; the latter is the minimum near $-10$ J.
The potential slope around $4$ cm is roughly $10$ J/cm, giving a force of roughly $1000$ N. With total energy zero, the minimum potential gives maximum kinetic energy about $10$ J.
Around $2$ cm the negative slope is of order $20$ J/cm. Converting units gives a force of order $2000$ N and acceleration of order $4000\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ for the $0.50$-kg object.

Measuring the actual source vector curve gives about $4.8\times10^3\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$ there; this is a graph approximation, rather than a supplied exact potential formula. Either estimate is incompatible with $4\,\mathrm{cm/s^2}=0.04\,\mathrm{m/s^2}$.
keyIdeas: Force is $-dU/dx$; kinetic energy is total energy minus potential energy.
commonMistakes: A slope in joules per centimeter must be multiplied by 100 to become newtons.
difficultyNotes: The question asks for the false statement. The graphical estimates should not be reported as exact physical data.

shortExplanation: In the uniform-disk stress model, both centrifugal loading and the supporting section area scale with thickness. The strength-limited specific energy therefore scales as tensile strength divided by density.
detailedSteps: A uniform disk has $I=Mr^2/2$, so its specific rotational energy is $K/M=r^2\omega^2/4$.
The outward centrifugal force on a half-disk scales as $\rho h\omega^2r^3$. The section carrying it has area proportional to $hr$, making the stress scale $\rho\omega^2r^2$; thickness cancels.
The strength limit consequently has $\rho\omega^2r^2=c\sigma$, where $c$ is a dimensionless stress-profile and material factor in this ideal disk model.
Substitution gives $K/M=(c/4)\sigma/\rho$. Absorb the factor into the stated dimensionless constant $\alpha$, giving option E.
Options C, D and E all have energy-per-mass units. Units alone are insufficient: the force-to-area thickness cancellation excludes the additional thickness factors in C and D.
keyIdeas: Combine specific rotational energy with the tensile-stress scaling.
commonMistakes: Do not claim that E is the only dimensionally valid option. A numerical strength coefficient requires more material information.
difficultyNotes: This is an ideal continuum-disk estimate. The unspecified dimensionless coefficient is not a numerical engineering failure criterion.

shortExplanation: The middle plot is a straight line when log(y) is graphed against x. Exponentiating that linear relation gives an exponential function.
detailedSteps: Using natural logarithms for the displayed positive data, write $\log y=c+bx$. Exponentiating gives $y=e^c e^{bx}=ae^{bx}$, with $a>0$.
A power law would instead make the log-log plot straight. That plot is curved in the actual source.
keyIdeas: Choose the transformation that makes the graph linear.
commonMistakes: A rapidly rising ordinary graph alone does not distinguish an exponential from a power law.
difficultyNotes: The straight semilog trend supplies the relevant evidence; the drawings do not provide exact numerical regression data.

shortExplanation: A displacement x raises one water surface and lowers the other, producing a 2x head difference. The restoring force acts on the inertia of the entire water column.
detailedSteps: Let the common tube area be $A$. The moving water has mass $M=\rho_w AL$.
In the standard vertical-arm small-displacement arrangement, the head difference is $2x$, so the restoring force is $F=-2\rho_w Agx$.
Thus $\ddot x=-(2g/L)x$. Angular frequency is $\sqrt{2g/L}$, and ordinary frequency is $f=(1/2\pi)\sqrt{2g/L}$.
keyIdeas: Both free surfaces contribute to the restoring head.
commonMistakes: Density and area cancel; the angular frequency still needs division by $2\pi$.
difficultyNotes: Small displacement keeps the surfaces in the operating vertical arms, while the whole column contributes inertia.

shortExplanation: In the usual operating geometry, the oil occupies one vertical arm. Its density is half the water density, so its L-height column balances a water head L/2; the free surfaces differ by L/2.
detailedSteps: Take the oil-water interface as the reference level. An oil column of vertical height $L$ supplies gauge pressure $\rho_o gL=(\rho_w/2)gL$.
The water free surface must therefore be at height $H_w=L/2$ above that interface. The oil free surface is at height $H_o=L$.
The free-surface difference is $H_o-H_w=L/2$.

This calculation uses the standard operating-arm interpretation of the stated U-tube: the added oil remains in a vertical arm. The source does not provide the bend or arm dimensions. If the interface enters a long bend, column length need not equal vertical head and more geometry would be needed.
keyIdeas: Compare pressure at the common interface, then subtract free-surface heights.
commonMistakes: The interface-to-water height is not the oil column height.
difficultyNotes: The vertical-arm geometry is an explicit model scope, not an additional printed dimension.

shortExplanation: Each bounce multiplies the next flight time by 0.9. The infinitely many shrinking flights have a finite total duration of 100 seconds.
detailedSteps: A launch upward at speed $u$ returns to the same height after $2u/g$. The successive launch speeds are $50,50(0.9),50(0.9)^2,\ldots$.
The corresponding total flight time is $$T=\frac{2(50)}{10}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(0.9)^n=\frac{10}{1-0.9}=100\,\mathrm{s}.$$
No finite-numbered bounce has zero outgoing speed. Instead, the collision times accumulate at $T=100$ while every remaining speed and flight height tend to zero.

The natural classical contact completion is rest at ground after this accumulation time, with the normal force supporting the weight. This uses the specified ideal instantaneous impacts and introduces no small-bounce cutoff.
keyIdeas: An infinite number of events can occupy a finite time.
Check the limiting position and speed when completing the ideal motion.
commonMistakes: Concluding infinite time from infinitely many bounces ignores convergence of the geometric series.
difficultyNotes: The rest state occurs at the limit of the shrinking flights, rather than at a last finite bounce.

shortExplanation: Small slopes allow lossless rolling, giving a constant total energy mgh. Above the no-slip threshold, sliding dissipates energy; the energy decreases continuously, then returns toward mgh as normal force vanishes near vertical.
detailedSteps: For the usual centered-ball model, write $I=\beta mR^2$ with $\beta>0$. No-slip motion needs friction $f=\beta mg\sin\theta/(1+\beta)$, so it is possible while $\tan\theta\leq\mu(1+\beta)/\beta$. Static friction then does no work and total kinetic energy is $mgh$.
Above that threshold, the common coefficient gives sliding acceleration $a=g(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)>0$ and angular acceleration $\dot\omega=\mu g\cos\theta/(\beta R)$.

For travel distance $h/\sin\theta$, use $t^2=2h/[g\sin\theta(\sin\theta-\mu\cos\theta)]$. With $z=\mu\cot\theta$, the total energy becomes $$\frac{K}{mgh}=1-z+\frac{z^2}{\beta(1-z)},\qquad 0<z<\frac{\beta}{1+\beta}.$$
At the threshold $z=\beta/(1+\beta)$ the expression equals 1, so there is no jump. Equal static and kinetic coefficients are essential to this continuity.

The derivative with respect to $z$ is $-1+(2z-z^2)/[\beta(1-z)^2]$. It has a single minimum at $z=1-1/\sqrt{1+\beta}$. As the angle grows, $z$ decreases from the threshold to zero: energy first falls, then rises back to 1 near vertical. This is graph C.

The plotted dip describes positive friction. If $\mu=0$, all angles instead give $K=mgh$: the dip collapses to a flat degenerate limit. Strict positive friction is not separately printed, so this boundary case is retained explicitly.
keyIdeas: Include rotational energy and verify the transition between rolling and sliding.
The qualitative graph follows for any positive centered inertia ratio, without needing its numerical value.
commonMistakes: Graph D has an unphysical jump for equal friction coefficients. Friction tends to zero near a vertical incline, so the energy cannot tend to zero there.
difficultyNotes: The result is the generic positive-friction graph in the usual centered-ball model; the zero-friction boundary and mass-centering interpretation are explicit for review.

shortExplanation: The sticking impact gives the combined mass a downward speed. Its new equilibrium lies below the original supported position, so the largest displacement is the equilibrium shift plus the oscillation amplitude.
detailedSteps: Using the standard initially quiescent supported state, the falling mass reaches $u=\sqrt{2g(5)}=10\,\mathrm{m/s}$. Impulse momentum conservation gives the joined $8$-kg mass speed $V=2(10)/8=2.5\,\mathrm{m/s}$ downward.
The angular frequency after impact is $\omega=\sqrt{72/8}=3\,\mathrm{rad/s}$. The added weight shifts equilibrium downward by $d=2g/72=5/18\,\mathrm{m}$.
Immediately after impact, displacement from the new equilibrium is $-d$ and downward speed is $V$. The amplitude is $$A=\sqrt{d^2+(V/\omega)^2}=\frac{5\sqrt{10}}{18}\,\mathrm{m}.$$
The two extremes relative to the original position are $d\pm A$. The larger absolute value is $$d+A=\frac{5(1+\sqrt{10})}{18}=1.1562\ldots\,\mathrm{m},$$ nearest the listed $1.1$ meters.
The original spring compression is $6g/72=0.8333\ldots$ m. Even at the upper extreme, it remains compressed by $0.8333+d-A>0$, so the supported objects do not lose contact.

The source describes a supported body and its original location; the quiescent equilibrium interpretation is stated here. An initially oscillating supported body would need an additional initial phase and velocity.
keyIdeas: Separate the impulsive sticking event from subsequent energy-conserving oscillation.
Measure displacement relative to the requested original position.
commonMistakes: Amplitude alone is not the largest displacement from the old equilibrium. Energy is not conserved during the sticking impact.
difficultyNotes: The stationary supported initial state and continued positive spring compression are both identified explicitly.

shortExplanation: The thicker string supports proportionally more tension, but it also has proportionally more mass per unit length. Those area factors cancel in the wave speed.
detailedSteps: For cross-sectional area $A=\pi r^2$, the same steel has maximum tension $T_{\max}=\sigma A$ and linear mass density $M/L=\rho A$.
The specified wave relation gives $v=\sqrt{T_{\max}/(M/L)}=\sqrt{\sigma/\rho}$, independent of radius.
The equal lengths give the same fundamental $f=v/(2L)$, hence $f_1/f_2=1$.
keyIdeas: Breaking tension and linear mass density both scale with area.
commonMistakes: A fourfold radius is a sixteenfold area, but the frequency ratio still cancels to one.
difficultyNotes: The calculation uses the explicitly supplied no-stiffness, no-stretch wave model.

shortExplanation: In-phase motion leaves the central spring unchanged, while opposite-phase motion makes it contribute twice the end-spring restoring force. The squared frequencies differ by a factor of three.
detailedSteps: The equations for displacements from equilibrium are $m\ddot x_A=-2kx_A+kx_B$ and $m\ddot x_B=kx_A-2kx_B$.
For $x_A=x_B$, each becomes $\ddot x=-(k/m)x$, so $\omega_1=\sqrt{k/m}$.
For $x_B=-x_A$, each becomes $\ddot x=-(3k/m)x$, so $\omega_2=\sqrt{3k/m}$. Thus $\omega_2/\omega_1=\sqrt3$.
keyIdeas: Use the actual in-phase and opposite-phase eigenvectors.
commonMistakes: For opposite motion the central spring changes length by twice either cart displacement.
difficultyNotes: Suitable small-amplitude initial conditions excite either pure mode without cart collisions.
